By Josh Pilcher

Physics is not impressed. A Starship stack leaves the pad. The power in this picture is real. So is the arithmetic that governs where it can go, and the arithmetic does not care who built the rocket.

Latest Report · Tuesday, November 10, 2026

Physics Is Not Impressed

Elon Musk can talk an engineer into moving a mountain. He cannot talk the rocket equation into moving. What he wants, what he believes, and the exact places where the universe sends the bill.

Elon Musk does not run a portfolio of companies. He runs two projects, a second planet and a post-carbon Earth, with the largest private fortune in history as their working capital. He believes the destinations; on that, the record is not close. What he does not believe is his own calendar. Delivered hardware arrives about twice as late as promised, and every Mars date he has ever given has missed by at least one full 26-month launch window.

Physics does not forbid Mars. It prices it, in tanker flights by the dozen and reliability proven across hundreds of flights, neither of which exists yet. On the ground the legend mostly collapses: the affordable car was killed by cost, the robotaxi is waiting on statistical proof, and only the robot, Optimus, is truly fighting physics, carrying about three hours of hard work in its chest. Texas, the ground he chose for all of it, replaced its government last week.

Read the full report →

Physics Is Not Impressed · Evening Report

Four numbers, one argument

The fortune is fuel, the pace is real, the price list is exponential, and the robot’s lunchbox is too small.

$11.4BThe cash engine
Starlink revenue in 2025, with $4.4 billion of operating income: the only profitable segment at SpaceX, and the money that funds the Mars ship.
165Launches in 2025
Falcon flights in a single year, lofting 2,213 tons: more than 80 percent of all the mass humanity put into orbit.
808The denominator
Consecutive successful flights needed to prove NASA’s 1-in-270 crew safety standard at 95 percent confidence. Starship has flown 14 times.
2.3 kWhThe robot’s lunchbox
Optimus’s entire battery. At a working draw of 500 to 700 watts that is three to four and a half hours, priced by chemistry improving 3 to 5 percent a year.

The slip factor

How long delivery actually took, divided by the first promised span. Delivered hardware clusters near two. Starship’s first orbit is in a class of its own.

The pattern is the finding of Chapter Two: the destination record and the deadline record are different datasets. Read his hardware dates multiplied by about two, and his Mars dates plus a full 26-month window.

Inside the Report
01 The Verdict

The Bottom Line

He believes the destinations and treats the dates as a tool. Physics prices Mars in tanker flights and 808-flight denominators. On the ground, the car was killed by cost, the robotaxi waits on proof, and only the robot is truly fighting physics.

 $180MHis whole fortune, bet in 2008→ 02 Chapter One

What He Actually Wants

Two projects, written down in 2006 and never revised since: a second planet, and an Earth that runs on sunlight. Every company he runs is an organ of one of them, and the fortune is their working capital.

 $11.4BStarlink revenue, 2025→ 03 Chapter Two

The Destination Is Real. The Dates Are a Tool.

The destinations have not moved in twenty-four years. The deadlines move constantly, and they tend to move near moments when confidence is worth money. In 2008 he bet everything. That part is real too.

 14.0xStarship orbit slip factor→ 04 Chapter Three

The Pace, In Numbers

Falcon is an operating fact, proven across more than 700 flights. Starship is fourteen flights and a first orbit six weeks old. The distance between those two numbers is where all the bad forecasts live.

 2,213 tMass to orbit, 2025→ 05 Chapter Four

The Price List

Delta-v, a chemical ceiling the best engine ever flown already touches, a calendar that opens every 26 months, air too thin to land in, and a fuel plant five orders of magnitude short of the requirement.

 9.4 km/sThe price of orbit alone→ 06 Chapter Five

The Battery Wall, and the Robot

The car was killed by cost, not physics: the $25,000 Tesla shipped at $36,990, decontented. The robot is the opposite case, and its arithmetic is the harshest in the report.

 232.5Wh/kg, the 4680 cell, measured→ 07 Chapter Six

The One Fight That Is Not Physics

Fog blinds cameras and lidar alike; the sensor that survives fog is the radar Tesla deleted. The binding constraint is proof, and proof is priced in billions of miles.

 11B miRAND’s price of proof→ 08 Chapter Seven

Houston, Then Texas

Johnson Space Center is shrinking and still runs the crewed program from Houston. Starbase flies at a fifth of its permit. And on November 3, the state replaced the government his Texas position was built with.

 25/yrStarbase’s launch license→ 09 Chapter Eight

Two Rival Reads

Two honest ways to read everything above. Physics permits it, on physics’ schedule, or the wall is the chain and the ledger and physics is the alibi. Each names the dated evidence that would prove it.

 2028The year both reads get graded→ 10 Chapter Nine

The Local Desk

Houston first: the old space age is changing jobs. Then Texas, the ground he chose for the whole empire, which changed its government last week.

Chapter Seven · Houston, Then Texas

The ground he chose, repriced

Johnson Space Center’s civil workforce fell 16 percent in a year, to 2,643, while Mission Control ran the first crewed flight around the Moon since Apollo. The building and flying are migrating to companies. Houston’s leverage now runs through Congress and contracts.

THE BOARDPURPOSE

Why The Board exists.

By Josh Pilcher

I don’t have a ton of time. It’s hard to keep up.

There are so many conflicting narratives, fed by conflicting interests. It feels hard to know what is true, and I know I’m not alone in that.

I often have questions I want answered, or things I don’t understand, that the news simply doesn’t cover. Not all of the time, but sometimes. When that happens, there is nowhere obvious to go for a straight answer.

In my ideal world, I build something useful to me. Something I enjoy reading. Because if I do, so will other people, and it will help them too.

What that looks like in a year, who knows.

The Board is a personal project. Everything here reflects my own views and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or representative of my employer.

From the Latest Report

What to watch next

Five things that settle the argument, in the order they arrive:

  1. 1Nov 13, 2026 · Starship Flight 15The first attempted catch of a returning ship, with a V3 booster catch alongside and 26 more Starlink V3 satellites aboard. Musk rates the ship catch at 50 to 60 percent on the first try.
  2. 2Nov 30, 2026 · Starbase review comments closeThe FAA’s environmental review of 100, then 456, launches a year takes public comment until November 30. Whether the study survives scoping sets Starbase’s ceiling for the decade.
  3. 3Early 2027 · Ship-to-ship refueling demoThe single test underneath every Moon and Mars date in the report. Tonnes transferred, boiloff measured over weeks, and a repeat performance are the facts that matter.
  4. 42028 · The Artemis IV refueling countCount the flights it actually takes to fill one lander. Near six to eight, his numbers were right and the panels were timid. In the high teens, the compound-closure read wins.
  5. 5End of 2027 · Optimus goes on sale, or doesn’tExternal deliveries at a stated price, with a published unit count, make it a product. Another year of internal pilots makes it a program. Watch the older cars’ hardware remedy alongside it.
